Vassalage is the word for a relationship of dependence and submission between a weaker party and a more powerful one — where the weaker party gives loyalty, service, and obedience in exchange for protection or land. Think of it as an unequal deal between two parties, where one side is clearly "above" and the other is clearly "below."

To truly understand vassalage, you need to picture medieval Europe — kingdoms, knights, castles, and lords. Society at that time was built on a pyramid of power, a system historians call feudalism. At the very top sat a king. Below the king were powerful nobles — dukes, counts, barons. Below them were smaller knights and landholders. And below everyone were the common people.

In this world, land was everything. It meant wealth, food, soldiers, and power. But no single person could control and defend vast stretches of land alone. So lords made deals. A lord would grant a piece of land, called a fief, to a man willing to serve him. That man would then kneel before the lord in a formal ceremony, swear an oath of loyalty, and become his vassal. The act of kneeling and swearing was called homage, and the formal oath of loyalty was called fealty.

Once that oath was taken, the relationship they now shared — the whole arrangement binding them together — was called vassalage.
What vassalage actually meant in practice

Vassalage was not just a moment or a ceremony. It was an ongoing condition — a permanent state of duty and obligation. The vassal, as long as he lived under that agreement, was expected to fight for his lord when called upon, provide soldiers from his own land, attend the lord's court, give him counsel, and sometimes pay financial dues. He could not simply walk away from these obligations without breaking his oath, which was considered a grave betrayal and could cost him everything — his land, his honor, or even his life.

In return, the lord had obligations too. He was supposed to protect his vassal, defend him from enemies, and grant him justice. The deal only worked because both sides had something to gain — and something to lose if they broke it.

So when we say someone lived "in vassalage," it means they lived in this state of formal, sworn subordination to another — bound by duty, loyalty, and dependence.
The bigger picture: chains of vassalage

One of the most fascinating things about vassalage is that it could stack. A duke might be the vassal of a king, while at the same time being the lord of a dozen lesser knights — who were, in turn, his vassals. So the same person could be both a lord and a vassal depending on who you were measuring against. This created long, interlocking chains of loyalty and duty running all the way up and down medieval society. Vassalage was not just a personal relationship — it was the glue that held the entire social and political order together.

The figurative meaning — and why you'll see this word outside of history

Today, vassalage doesn't only appear in history books. It is regularly used in a figurative sense to describe any situation — political, international, or personal — where one party is so dependent on, or dominated by, another that it resembles the old medieval arrangement, even if no oaths or land are involved.

For example, if a small, weak country is forced to follow the decisions of a much larger, powerful neighbor — even without any formal agreement — writers and commentators might describe that small country as being in a state of vassalage. They mean: it is behaving like a vassal, submitting to a stronger power out of dependence or fear rather than true choice.

Similarly, if a person is entirely controlled by someone else and has little freedom to make independent decisions, their condition could metaphorically be called vassalage.

The key feeling the word always carries — whether used literally or figuratively — is one of subjugation, dependence, and the absence of full freedom or equality. There is always someone above, and the vassal is always, in some meaningful way, beneath them.
The range of what vassalage can refer to

The word can refer to any of these related but distinct things, and context will tell you which one is meant:

The condition of being a vassal — the state of subordination itself. ("He spent his life in vassalage.")

The duties and obligations that come with being a vassal — the actual service owed. ("The vassalage required him to provide forty knights every summer.")

The system or institution of vassalage as a whole — meaning the broader feudal arrangement that made the entire lord-vassal dynamic possible and socially recognized. ("Vassalage was the foundation of medieval political life.")

A group of vassals collectively — sometimes the word is used to describe all the vassals under a lord taken together. ("The king called upon his vassalage to assemble.")
The one core idea to always remember

No matter the context, vassalage always points to the same essential reality: a structured, often formalized relationship in which one party surrenders a degree of independence and owes submission and service to another, typically in exchange for protection, land, or some other form of support. It is power made into a relationship — unequal, binding, and deeply consequential for everyone within it.
